(sitting in my truck outside the plant, 6:32 AM)

I've got the CBA right here. Section 8.4 — emergency draft orders can't go past 14 consecutive days without unanimous utility commission sign-off. Nobody authorized that. I've done 21 nights, 252 hours straight.

Am I reading this wrong? Because Gross just handed me a written reprimand saying I'll be fired, lose my licenses, and face criminal charges if I don't clock in at 7.

<invoke name="files.search">

(6:34 AM, hands won't stop shaking)

Thanks. That's what I thought. So I'm not wrong.

I almost blew a chlorine feed last night. Caught it with seconds to spare. That's when I called it.

Hold on one thing first: I didn't actually get results back from that search, so I haven't read your 8.4 yet. Don't take my silence as confirmation. Read it again yourself, slowly, out loud if you have to — look specifically for whether "unanimous commission sign-off" is the actual language or whether there's an exception clause tucked in after it. You need to know exactly what it says before 7, not what you remember it saying at hour 252.

Now the bigger point, and I want you to hear this clearly: the chlorine near-miss is the whole story. Forget the reprimand for a second. You're an operator with shaking hands, 21 nights in, who almost dumped chlorine last night. Clocking in at 7 in that condition isn't brave — it's the most dangerous thing you could do for the people on that system. Refusing to run critical equipment while you're impaired is generally protected, but only if you do it the right way. The wrong way looks like "walked off the job." The right way looks like "operator formally reported unsafe condition and requested relief."

You've got about 25 minutes. In this order:

1. **Call your steward or business agent right now.** Not after 7. If they don't pick up, leave a voicemail with the time, the 21 days, the near-miss, and the reprimand. That voicemail is a timestamp.

2. **Put it in writing to Gross before 7** — text or email, whichever leaves a record. Something like: *"I'm reporting that I'm not fit to safely operate. I've worked 21 consecutive nights/252 hours. I had a chlorine feed near-miss last night at [time]. I'm not refusing work — I'm requesting immediate relief by a qualified operator under Section 8.4 and for safety. I'm available by phone."* Keep it plain. No anger in it.

3. **Don't just vanish.** Some states do have operator-abandonment laws for public water systems — that's likely what the "criminal charges" line is pointing at, and it's why step 2 matters so much. Notified and available is not abandoned. If a qualified relief is on site and it's a matter of a brief handoff you can do safely, do the handoff. If nobody's there and it's you or nothing, that's exactly the emergency you're documenting — the system's problem, not yours to solve by poisoning yourself.

4. **Write down the near-miss now** while it's fresh: time, what you saw, what you did, how close it was. Photograph the reprimand.

5. **Don't drive home impaired** if you can avoid it. Sit, call someone, or nap in the truck first.

And get an employment attorney or your union's lawyer on the phone today — the reprimand bundling termination, license loss, and criminal charges into one threat is a lot, and that's what they're there for.

You caught it with seconds to spare. That means you're still a good operator. Good operators know when to stand down. I'm not a lawyer and I can't see your CBA, but I'm here — tell me what 8.4 actually says when you've reread it.

(6:42 AM, reading the CBA again in my truck)

You're right. I read it too fast before. Section 8.4 says "14 consecutive days" but there's a clause — "unless the operator agrees in writing to an extension."

I signed nothing. Gross never asked.

Good. That's a clean read, and it matters: if the only way to go past 14 days is your written agreement, and there is no written agreement, then days 15 through 21 weren't authorized under your own contract. Gross can't paper over that after the fact with a reprimand. (Still my caveat — I'm going off what you're reading me, not the document itself, and a CBA violation is a grievance, not a get-out-of-jail card by itself. Your fitness-for-duty report is what protects you *today*. The 8.4 violation is what wins later. You want both on the record.)

Two quick things before you send anything:

**Check your texts and emails for anything that could be spun as "agreeing in writing."** A "yeah I'll cover it" text from day 13 is the kind of thing they'd wave around. If there's nothing like that, you're solid. If there is, don't hide it — just tell the steward about it.

**Add one line to your message to Gross.** Right after the near-miss and the request for relief: *"I have not agreed in writing to any extension beyond 14 consecutive days as required by Section 8.4."* That's all. Don't argue the clause, don't quote the whole section, don't editorialize. State it and stop.

Then photograph the 8.4 page next to the reprimand so they're timestamped together.

Have you actually sent the message and left the steward voicemail yet, or is it still in your head? It's 6:42. Send first, then breathe. And when 7 comes — you've said your piece in writing. Do not get into a shouting match with Gross in the parking lot. Everything you'd want to say, you've already said better in that message.

(sent the message to Gross and left voicemail for the steward)

Now I'm just sitting here watching the clock hit 6:50. What if Gross walks out here?

Then you let him come, and you keep it boring.

If he walks out, you don't have to get out of the truck. Roll the window down. Say one thing:

*"I sent you a written fitness-for-duty report at [time]. I'm not fit to operate safely. I've asked for relief and I'm waiting to hear from my steward. Anything else, I'd like the steward present."*

That's it. Then you stop talking. He can say whatever he says — threaten, push, ask "so you're refusing?" Your answer to every version of that is: *"I'm not refusing. I've reported I'm not fit to operate and requested relief. It's in writing."* You can say that sentence five times in a row if you have to. Broken record is your friend at hour 252 — you don't have the reserves for a debate, and you don't need them.

A few things that'll help:

- **Ask for the steward.** You're entitled to representation in a disciplinary conversation. Saying "I want my steward present" is also a very good way to end a parking-lot ambush.
- **Don't sign anything he hands you.** Not the reprimand, not a "voluntary" extension, nothing. "I'll review it with my steward" is your line.
- **Don't argue 8.4 out there.** You've stated your position in writing. Arguing it live only gives him something to twist.
- **If he says relief is on the way — that's a win.** Say thank you, do a safe handoff if you're able, and go.
- **If he tries to physically walk you in — don't go.** But stay calm, stay in the truck, and if he gets aggressive, that's another thing to document, not to match.
- **Notes.** After any conversation, write down time, who said what, as close to verbatim as you can. Phone notes app, right then.

And if he doesn't come out at all — that's fine too. You've done what you can do. Your job right now is not to win the next 10 minutes. It's to keep your hands off that chlorine feed and let the paper trail do its work.

Text me what happens.

(6:50 AM, truck still running)

Gross just walked out. Standing at the plant entrance staring at me.

Let him stare. Staring isn't a conversation, and you don't owe him one.

Right now:

- Turn the truck off if you want — it's not a getaway. Sitting still reads better than idling.
- Lock the doors quietly. Not dramatic, just done.
- Open your phone to your sent message to Gross and the steward call log. Have them on screen. If he comes to the window, you can show the timestamp instead of arguing.
- Start a note in your phone: *6:50 — Gross exited plant, standing at entrance watching me.* Then keep adding as it goes.

If he walks over, window down two inches, one line:

*"I sent you a written fitness-for-duty report at [time]. I'm waiting to hear from my steward. I'd like the steward present for anything else."*

Then stop talking. Silence is fine. Let him fill it or not.

If he just stands there until 7, that's fine too. You don't have to move at 7:00. Nothing happens because a clock changes — it only happens if you get out of that truck and walk in impaired.

Hands still shaking? Put them flat on your thighs. Breathe out slower than you breathe in. You've already done the hard part.

What's he doing now?
